The algebro-geometric solutions for the modified Camassa-Holm hierarchy

Yu Hou    Engui Fan Note: Corresponding author and e-mail address: faneg@fudan.edu.cn    Zhijun Qiao
1 School of Mathematical Sciences, Institute of Mathematics
and Key Laboratory of Mathematics for Nonlinear Science,
Fudan University, Shanghai 200433, P.R. China
2 Department of Mathematics, University of Texas-Pan American,
Edinburg, TX 78539, U.S.A
Abstract

This paper is dedicated to provide theta function representation of algebro-geometric solutions and related crucial quantities for the modified Camassa-Holm (MCH) hierarchy through studying a algebro-geometric initial value problem. Our main tools include the polynomial recursive formalism to derive the MCH hierarchy, the hyperelliptic curve with finite number of genus, the Baker-Akhiezer functions, the meromorphic function, the Dubrovin-type equations for auxiliary divisors, and the associated trace formulas. With the help of these tools, the explicit representations of the Baker-Ahhiezer functions, the meromorphic function, and the algebro-geometric solutions are obtained for the entire MCH hierarchy.

1 Introduction

Algebro-geometric solution, an important feature of integrable system, is a kind of explicit solutions closely related to the inverse spectral theory [1],[4],[6]-[8]. As a degenerated case of the algebro-geometric solution, the multi-soliton solution and periodic solution in elliptic function type may be obtained [4],[5],[21]. A systematic approach, proposed by Gesztesy and Holden to construct algebro-geometric solutions for integrable equations, has been extended to the whole (1+1) dimensional integrable hierarchy, such as the AKNS hierarchy, the Camassa-Holm (CH) hierarchy etc. [9]-[12]. Recently, we investigated the Gerdjikov-Ivanov hierarchy and the Degasperis-Procesi hierarchy and obtained their algebro-geometric solutions [15],[16].

The CH equation

ut−ux​x​t+2​γ​ux+3​u​ux−2​ux​ux​x−u​ux​x​x=0u_{t}-u_{xxt}+2\gamma u_{x}+3uu_{x}-2u_{x}u_{xx}-uu_{xxx}=0 (1.1)

where γ\gamma is a real constant, was derived from the two-dimensional Euler equations in a search for integrable shallow water equations, with the u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) is the fluid velocity in the xx direction and γ\gamma is a constant related to the critical shallow water wave speed [2]. The CH equation describes the propagation of two-dimensional shallow water waves over a flat bed, also the propagation of axially symmetric waves in hyperelastic rods [20],[22]. The CH and the Degasperis-Procesi (DP) equations are only two integrable members with b=2b=2 and b=3b=3 from the following family

ut−ut​x​x+γ​b​ux+(b+1)​u​ux=b​ux​ux​x+u​ux​x​x,u_{t}-u_{txx}+\gamma bu_{x}+(b+1)uu_{x}=bu_{x}u_{xx}+uu_{xxx}, (1.2)

where bb is a constant.

Due to its many remarkable integrable properties, the CH equation has extensively been studied in the last twenty years. The bi-Hamiltonian structure of the CH equation was implied in the work of Fuchssteiner and Fokas [14].Complete integrability and infinity of conservation laws have been studied in [2],[3],[28]. The inverse scattering transform was developed by Constantin, McKean, Gerdjikov and Ivanov [23],[24]. Other progress in studying the CH equation includes the existence of peaked solitons and geometry of multi-peakons [2],[29], geometric formulations [26], and waves breaking [25]. The classic papers on the algebro-geometric solutions of the CH equation, or more appropriately, one is due to Qiao, the other is Gesztesy and Holden. Qiao obtained the algebro-geometric solution on a symplectic submainfold [19]. Gesztesy and Holden derived the algebro-geometric solutions for the whole CH hierarchy by using the polynomial recursion method [10]-[12].

This paper is concerned with the following equation, called the modified Camassa-Holm (MCH) equation

ut−ux​x​t+3​u2​ux−ux3=(4​u−2​ux​x)​ux​ux​x+(u2−ux2)​ux​x​x,u_{t}-u_{xxt}+3u^{2}u_{x}-u_{x}^{3}=(4u-2u_{xx})u_{x}u_{xx}+(u^{2}-u_{x}^{2})u_{xxx}, (1.3)

where u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) is the function of spatial variable xx and time variable tt. For our convenience, let us rewrite (1.3) as

qt+qx​(u2−ux2)+2​q2​ux=0,q_{t}+q_{x}(u^{2}-u_{x}^{2})+2q^{2}u_{x}=0, (1.4)
q=u−ux​x.q=u-u_{xx}. (1.5)

The MCH equation (1.3) was derived as an integrable system by Fuchssteiner, and Olver and Rosenau by applying the tri-Hamiltonian method to the representation of the modified KdV equation [13],[31]. Later, Qiao recovered the MCH equation (1.3) from the two-dimensional Euler equations by using the approximation procedure, provided the Lax pair and bi-Hamiltonian structure for the MCH equation, and first time proposed the W/M-shape solitons [17]. Recently, Gui, Liu, Olver and Qu showed the wave-breaking and peaked traveling-wave solutions for the MCH equation [30]. However, within the knowledge of the authors, the algebro-geometric solutions of the entire MCH hierarchy are not studied yet.

The main task of this paper focuses on the algebro-geometric solutions of the whole MCH hierarchy in which (1.3) is just the second member. The outline of the present paper is as follows.

In section 2, based on the polynomial recursion formalism, we derive the MCH hierarchy, the associated sequences, and Lax pairs. A hyper-elliptic curve 𝒦n\mathcal{K}_{n} with arithmetic genus nn is introduced with the help of the characteristic polynomial of Lax matrix VnV_{n} for the stationary MCH hierarchy.

In Section 3, we study a meromorphic function ϕ\phi such that ϕ\phi satisfies a nonlinear second-order differential equation. Then we study the properties of the Baker-Akhiezer function ψ\psi, and furthermore the stationary MCH equations are decomposed into a system of Dubrovin-type equations. The stationary trace formulas are obtained for the MCH hierarchy.

In Section 4, we present the first set of our results, the explicit theta function representations of Baker-Akhiezer function, the meromorphic function and the potentials uu for the entire stationary MCH hierarchy. Furthermore, we study the initial value problem on an algebro-geometric curve for the stationary MCH hierarchy.

In Sections 5 and 6, we extend the analysis in Sections 3 and 4 to the time-dependent case. Each equation in the MCH hierarchy is permitted to evolve in terms of an independent time parameter trt_{r}. As an initial data we use a stationary solution of the nnth equation and then construct a time-dependent solution of the rrth equation in the MCH hierarchy. The Baker-Akhiezer function, the meromorphic function, the analogs of the Dubrovin-type equations, the trace formulas, and the theta function representation in Section 4 are all extended to the time-dependent case.

2 The MCH hierarchy

In this section, let us derive the MCH hierarchy and the corresponding sequence of zero-curvature pairs by using a polynomial recursion formalism. Moreover, we introduce the hyper-elliptic curve connecting to the stationary MCH hierarchy.

Throughout this section, let us make the following hypothesis.

Hypothesis 2.1

In the stationary case, let us assume

u∈C∞(ℂ),∂xku∈L∞(ℂ),k∈ℕ0.\begin{split}&u\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{C}),\ \ \partial_{x}^{k}u\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{C}),\qquad k\in\mathbb{N}_{0}.\end{split} (2.1)

u(⋅,t)∈C∞(ℂ),∂xku(⋅,t)∈L∞(ℂ),k∈ℕ0,t∈ℂ,u⁡(x,⋅),ux​x​(x,⋅)∈C1​(ℂ).\begin{split}&u(\cdot,t)\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{C}),\ \ \partial_{x}^{k}u(\cdot,t)\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{C}),\qquad k\in\mathbb{N}_{0},~~t\in\mathbb{C},\\ &u(x,\cdot),u_{xx}(x,\cdot)\in C^{1}(\mathbb{C}).\\ \end{split} (2.2)

where δ2​l\delta_{2l} are determined by the following formulas (for details, see [18])

δ2=2​u,δ2​l+2=𝒢(δ2​l),l∈ℕ,𝒢=−e−x∂−1e2​x∂−1e−x(u−ux​x)∂−1(u−ux​x)∂.\begin{split}&\delta_{2}=2u,\\ &\delta_{2l+2}=\mathcal{G}(\delta_{2l}),\qquad l\in\mathbb{N},\\ &\mathcal{G}=-e^{-x}\partial^{-1}e^{2x}\partial^{-1}e^{-x}(u-u_{xx})\partial^{-1}(u-u_{xx})\partial.\end{split} (2.4)

Apparently, the first few can be computed as follows:

where {cl}l∈ℕ0⊂ℂ\{c_{l}\}_{l\in\mathbb{N}_{0}}\subset\mathbb{C} are integration constants.

f2​l=∑k=0lcl−k​f^2​k,g2​l=∑k=0lcl−k​g^2​k,h2​l=∑k=0lcl−k​h^2​k,l∈ℕ0,f_{2l}=\sum_{k=0}^{l}c_{l-k}\hat{f}_{2k},\quad g_{2l}=\sum_{k=0}^{l}c_{l-k}\hat{g}_{2k},\quad h_{2l}=\sum_{k=0}^{l}c_{l-k}\hat{h}_{2k},\quad l\in\mathbb{N}_{0}, (2.7)

that is

into (2.26), we obtain

The stationary MCH hierarchy is defined by (2.28). The first few equations are

s−MCH0​(u)=2​ux−2​ux​x=0,s−MCH1​(u)=(ux−ux​x​x)​(u2−ux2)+2​(u−ux​x)2​ux+(ux−ux​x​x)​c1=0,etc.\begin{split}&\mathrm{s-MCH}_{0}(u)=2u_{x}-2u_{xx}=0,\\ &\mathrm{s-MCH}_{1}(u)=(u_{x}-u_{xxx})(u^{2}-u_{x}^{2})+2(u-u_{xx})^{2}u_{x}+(u_{x}-u_{xxx})c_{1}=0,\\ &\mathrm{etc}.\end{split} (2.29)

By definition, the set of solutions of (2.28) represents a class of algebro-geometric MCH solutions with nn ranging in ℕ0\mathbb{N}_{0} and clc_{l} in ℂ,l∈ℕ\mathbb{C},~l\in\mathbb{N}. We call the stationary algebro-geometric MCH solutions uu as MCH potentials at times.

Remark 2.2

Here we emphasize that if uu satisfies one of the stationary MCH equations in (2.28)(\ref{2.28}), then it must satisfy infinitely many such equations with order higher than nn for certain choices of integration constants clc_{l}. This is a common characteristic of the general integrable soliton equations such as the KdV, AKNS and CH hierarchies [12].

Next, we introduce the following homogeneous polynomials F^l,G^l,H^l\widehat{F}_{l},\widehat{G}_{l},\widehat{H}_{l} defined by

F^l(λ)=Fl(λ)|ck=0,k=1,…,l=∑k=0lf^2​kλ2​(l−k),l=0,…,n,\widehat{F}_{l}(\lambda)=F_{l}(\lambda)|_{c_{k}=0,~k=1,\dots,l}=\sum_{k=0}^{l}\hat{f}_{2k}\lambda^{2(l-k)},\qquad l=0,\ldots,n, (2.30)

−12​(utn−ux​x​tn)−h2​n,x+h2​n+(u−ux​x)​g2​n=0.\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2}(u_{t_{n}}-u_{xxt_{n}})-h_{2n,x}+h_{2n}+(u-u_{xx})g_{2n}=0. (2.41)

Hence, by (2.39) and (2.40), (2.41) can be rewritten as

MCHn​(u)=utn−ux​x​tn−2​f2​n,x=0,(x,tn)∈ℂ2,n∈ℕ0.\mathrm{MCH}_{n}(u)=u_{t_{n}}-u_{xxt_{n}}-2f_{2n,x}=0,\qquad(x,t_{n})\in\mathbb{C}^{2},~n\in\mathbb{N}_{0}. (2.42)

Varying n∈ℕ0n\in\mathbb{N}_{0} in (2.42) defines the time-dependent MCH hierarchy. The first few equations are

MCH0​(u)=ut0−ux​x​t0+2​ux−2​ux​x=0,MCH1​(u)=ut1−ux​x​t1+(ux−ux​x​x)​(u2−ux2)+2​(u−ux​x)2​ux+(ux−ux​x​x)​c1=0,etc.\begin{split}&\mathrm{MCH}_{0}(u)=u_{t_{0}}-u_{xxt_{0}}+2u_{x}-2u_{xx}=0,\\ &\mathrm{MCH}_{1}(u)=u_{t_{1}}-u_{xxt_{1}}+(u_{x}-u_{xxx})(u^{2}-u_{x}^{2})+2(u-u_{xx})^{2}u_{x}\\ &~~~~~~~~~~~~~+(u_{x}-u_{xxx})c_{1}=0,\\ &\mathrm{etc}.\end{split} (2.43)

The second equation MCH1​(u)=0\mathrm{MCH}_{1}(u)=0 (with c1=0c_{1}=0) in the hierarchy represents the Modified Camassa-Holm (MCH) equation as discussed in section 1. Similarly, one can introduce the corresponding homogeneous MCH hierarchy by

MCH^n​(u)=MCHn​(u)|cl=0,l=1,…,n=0,n∈ℕ0.\widehat{\mathrm{MCH}}_{n}(u)=\mathrm{MCH}_{n}(u)|_{c_{l}=0,~l=1,\ldots,n}=0,\qquad n\in\mathbb{N}_{0}. (2.44)

The MCH hierarchy can also be defined in the form of h2​nh_{2n} for the relation h2​n=−f2​nh_{2n}=-f_{2n}. The integration constants cl=0c_{l}=0 l=1,…,nl=1,\ldots,n are taken to derive the Modified Camassa-Holm equation MCH1​(u)=0\mathrm{MCH}_{1}(u)=0.

In fact, since the Lenard operator recursion formalism is almost universally adopted in the contemporary literature on the integrable soliton equations, it might be worthwhile to adopt the alternative approach using the polynomial recursion relations.

3 The stationary MCH formalism

In this section, we focus our attention on the stationary case. By using the polynomial recursion formalism described in section 2, we define a fundamental meromorphic function ϕ⁡(P,x)\phi(P,x) on a hyper-elliptic curve 𝒦n\mathcal{K}_{n}. Moreover, we study the properties of the Baker-Akhiezer function ψ⁡(P,x,x0)\psi(P,x,x_{0}), Dubrovin-type equations, and trace formulas.

We emphasize that the analysis about the stationary case described in section 2 also holds here for the present context.

Let

z=λ2,E~m=Em2,z=\lambda^{2},~~~~\widetilde{E}_{m}=E_{m}^{2}, (3.1)

then the hyper-elliptic curve 𝒦n\mathcal{K}_{n} is given by (2.21). 𝒦n\mathcal{K}_{n} is compactified by joining a point at infinity, P∞P_{\infty}, but for our convenience, the compactification is still denoted by 𝒦n\mathcal{K}_{n}. Point PP on

𝒦n∖{P∞},\mathcal{K}_{n}\setminus\{P_{\infty}\},

is referred to a pair type P=(z,y⁡(P))P=(z,y(P)), where y⁡(⋅)y(\cdot) is the meromorphic function on 𝒦n\mathcal{K}_{n} satisfying

ℱn​(z,y​(P))=0.\mathcal{F}_{n}(z,y(P))=0.

The complex structure on 𝒦n\mathcal{K}_{n} is defined in the usual way by introducing local coordinates

ζQ0:P→(z−z0)\zeta_{Q_{0}}:P\rightarrow(z-z_{0})

near points

Q0=(z0,y⁡(Q0))∈𝒦n∖P0,P0=(0,y⁡(P0)),Q_{0}=(z_{0},y(Q_{0}))\in\mathcal{K}_{n}\setminus P_{0},\qquad P_{0}=(0,y(P_{0})),

which are neither branch nor singular points of 𝒦n\mathcal{K}_{n}. Near P0P_{0}, the local coordinates are

ζP0:P→z1/2;\zeta_{P_{0}}:P\rightarrow z^{1/2};

near the branch point P∞∈𝒦nP_{\infty}\in\mathcal{K}_{n}, the local coordinates are

ζP∞:P→z−1,\zeta_{P_{\infty}}:P\rightarrow z^{-1},

and also the similar case at branch and singular points of 𝒦n.\mathcal{K}_{n}. Thus, 𝒦n\mathcal{K}_{n} becomes a two-sheeted hyper-elliptic Riemann surface [27] with genus n∈ℕ0n\in\mathbb{N}_{0} (possibly with a singular affine part) in a standard manner.

We also notice that fixing the zeros E~1,…,E~2​n+1\widetilde{E}_{1},\ldots,\widetilde{E}_{2n+1} of R2​n+1R_{2n+1} discussed in (2.21) leads to the curve 𝒦n\mathcal{K}_{n} fixed. Then the integration constants c1,…,cnc_{1},\ldots,c_{n} in f2​nf_{2n} are uniquely determined, which are the symmetric functions of E~1,…,E~2​n+1\widetilde{E}_{1},\ldots,\widetilde{E}_{2n+1}.

The holomorphic map ∗,\ast, changing sheets, is defined by

∗:{𝒦n→𝒦n,OPENP=(z,yj​(z))→P∗=(z,yj+1​(mod​2))​(z)),j=0,1,\displaystyle\ast:\begin{cases}\mathcal{K}_{n}\rightarrow\mathcal{K}_{n},\\ P=(z,y_{j}(z))\rightarrow P^{\ast}=(z,y_{j+1(\mathrm{mod}~2)})(z)),\quad j=0,1,\end{cases}
P∗⁣∗:=(P∗)∗,etc.,\displaystyle P^{\ast\ast}:=(P^{\ast})^{\ast},\quad\mathrm{etc}., (3.2)

where yj​(z),j=0,1y_{j}(z),\,j=0,1 denote the two branches of y⁡(P)y(P) satisfying ℱn​(z,y)=0\mathcal{F}_{n}(z,y)=0.
Finally, positive divisors on 𝒦n\mathcal{K}_{n} of degree nn are denoted by

𝒟P1,…,Pn:{𝒦n→ℕ0,P→𝒟P1,…,Pn={ k if P occurs k times in {P1,…,Pn}, 0 if P∉{P1,…,Pn}.\mathcal{D}_{P_{1},\ldots,P_{n}}:\begin{cases}\mathcal{K}_{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{N}_{0},\\ P\rightarrow\mathcal{D}_{P_{1},\ldots,P_{n}}=\begin{cases}\textrm{ $k$ if $P$ occurs $k$ times in $\{P_{1},\ldots,P_{n}\},$}\\ \textrm{ $0$ if $P\notin$$\{P_{1},\ldots,P_{n}\}.$}\end{cases}\end{cases} (3.3)

For the notational simplicity, assume n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}. The case n=0n=0 is treated in Example 4.10.

Next, we define the stationary Baker-Akhiezer function ψ⁡(P,x,x0)\psi(P,x,x_{0}) on 𝒦n∖{P∞,P0}\mathcal{K}_{n}\setminus\{P_{\infty},P_{0}\} as follows

Remark 3.3

The definition of stationary Baker-Akhiezer function ψ\psi of the MCH hierarchy is analogous to that in the context of KdV or AKNS hierarchies. But the crucial difference is that P0P_{0} is an essential singularity of ψ\psi in the MCH hierarchy, which is the same as in the CH hierarchy, but different from the KdV or AKNS hierarchy. This fact will be shown in the asymptotic expansions of ψ\psi in next section.

Furthermore, we derive Dubrovin-type equations, which are first-order coupled systems of differential equations and govern the dynamics of the zeros μj​(x)\mu_{j}(x) and νj​(x)\nu_{j}(x) of Fn​(z,x)F_{n}(z,x) and Hn​(z,x)H_{n}(z,x) with respect to xx. We recall that the affine part of 𝒦n\mathcal{K}_{n} is nonsingular if

{E~m}m=1,…,2​n+1⊂ℂ,E~m≠E~m′for m≠m′,m,m′=1,…,2​n+1.\{\widetilde{E}_{m}\}_{m=1,\ldots,2n+1}\subset\mathbb{C},\quad\widetilde{E}_{m}\neq\widetilde{E}_{m^{\prime}}\quad\textrm{for $m\neq m^{\prime},~m,m^{\prime}=1,\ldots,2n+1$}. (3.42)

The trace formulas in the MCH hierarchy are implicit for the potential uu, which is apposed to the general integrable soliton equations such as KdV, AKNS and CH hierarchies. But this dose not affect to obtain the algebro-geometric solutions of the MCH hierarchy, and we can still construct uu from trace formulas.

4 Algebro-geometric solutions of the stationary MCH hierarchy

In this section, we continue our study of the stationary MCH hierarchy, and will obtain explicit Riemann theta function representations for the meromorphic function ϕ\phi, and in particular for the potentials uu of the stationary MCH hierarchy.

Let us begin with the asymptotic properties of ϕ\phi and ψj,j=1,2\psi_{j},j=1,2.

Remark 4.2

We notice the unusual fact: P0P_{0} is the essential singularity of ψj\psi_{j}, j=1,2j=1,2. From (4.5)(\ref{4.5}) and (4.6)(\ref{4.6}), the leading-order exponential term ψj\psi_{j}, j=1,2,j=1,2, near P0P_{0} is xx-dependent, which makes the problem worse. One can obtain the analogous result near P∞P_{\infty} as displayed in (4.3)(\ref{4.3}) and (4.4)(\ref{4.4}). This is in sharp contrast to standard Baker-Akhiezer functions that typically feature a linear behavior with respect to xx, such as exp⁡(c⁡(x−x0))\mathrm{exp}(c(x-x_{0})) and exp⁡(c⁡(x−x0)​ζ−1)\mathrm{exp}(c(x-x_{0})\zeta^{-1}) near P∞P_{\infty} and P0P_{0}, respectively.

From (3.19), 𝒟P0​ν¯^∼𝒟P∞​μ¯^\mathcal{D}_{P_{0}\underline{\hat{\nu}}}\sim\mathcal{D}_{P_{\infty}\underline{\hat{\mu}}}, and P∞=(P∞)∗∉{μ^1,⋯,μ^n}P_{\infty}=(P_{\infty})^{\ast}\notin\{\hat{\mu}_{1},\cdots,\hat{\mu}_{n}\}, based on some hypothesis of Theorem A. 31 [12], one can have 𝒟ν¯^∈Symn​(𝒦n)\mathcal{D}_{\underline{\hat{\nu}}}\in\textrm{Sym}^{n}(\mathcal{K}_{n}) is nonspecial. This argument is symmetric with respect to μ¯^\underline{\hat{\mu}} and ν¯^\underline{\hat{\nu}}. Thus, 𝒟μ¯^\mathcal{D}_{\underline{\hat{\mu}}} is nonspecial if and only if 𝒟ν¯^\mathcal{D}_{\underline{\hat{\nu}}} is.

Therefore, the divisor (3.19) of ϕ⁡(P,x)\phi(P,x) suggests considering expression of the following type

Let us now construct uu from trace formulas (3.51) and (3.52). By comparing (3.51) with (3.52), we have

Remark 4.12

The result in Theorem 4.114.11 is derived in terms of uu and {μj}j=1,⋯,n\{\mu_{j}\}_{j=1,\cdots,n}, but we can prove the analogous result in terms of uu and {νj}j=1,⋯,n\{\nu_{j}\}_{j=1,\cdots,n}.

Remark 4.13

Theorem 4.114.11 reveals that given 𝒦n\mathcal{K}_{n} and the initial condition μ¯^​(x0)=(μ^1​(x0),…,μ^n​(x0))∈Symn​(𝒦n)\underline{\hat{\mu}}(x_{0})=(\hat{\mu}_{1}(x_{0}),\ldots,\hat{\mu}_{n}(x_{0}))\in\mathrm{Sym}^{n}(\mathcal{K}_{n}), or equivalently, the auxiliary divisor 𝒟μ¯^​(x0)∈Symn​(𝒦n)\mathcal{D}_{\underline{\hat{\mu}}(x_{0})}\in\mathrm{Sym}^{n}(\mathcal{K}_{n}) at x=x0x=x_{0}, uu is uniquely determined in an open neighborhood Ω\Omega of x0x_{0} by (4.58)(\ref{4.58}) and satisfies the nnth stationary MCH equation (2.28)(\ref{2.28}). Conversely, given 𝒦n\mathcal{K}_{n} and uu in an open neighborhood Ω\Omega of x0x_{0}, we can construct the corresponding polynomial Fn​(z,x)F_{n}(z,x), Gn​(z,x)G_{n}(z,x) and Hn​(z,x)H_{n}(z,x) for x∈Ωx\in\Omega, and then obtain the auxiliary divisor 𝒟μ¯^​(x)\mathcal{D}_{\underline{\hat{\mu}}(x)} for x∈Ωx\in\Omega from the zeros of Fn​(z,x)F_{n}(z,x) and (3.13)(\ref{3.13}). In that sense, once the curve 𝒦n\mathcal{K}_{n} is fixed, elements of the isospectral class of the MCH potentials uu can be characterized by nonspecial auxiliary divisor 𝒟μ¯^​(x)\mathcal{D}_{\underline{\hat{\mu}}(x)}.

5 The time-dependent MCH formalism

In this section, let us go back to the recursive approach detailed in Section 2 and extend the algebro-geometric analysis in Section 3 to the time-dependent MCH hierarchy.

Throughout this section, we assume that (2.2) holds.

The time-dependent algebro-geometric initial value problem of the MCH hierarchy is to solve the time-dependent rrth MCH flow with a stationary solution of the nnth equation as the initial data in the hierarchy. More precisely, given n∈ℕ0n\in\mathbb{N}_{0}, based on the solution u(0)u^{(0)} of the nnth stationary MCH equation s−MCHn​(u(0))=0\mathrm{s-MCH}_{n}(u^{(0)})=0 associated with 𝒦n\mathcal{K}_{n} and a set of integration constants {cl}l=1,…,n⊂ℂ\{c_{l}\}_{l=1,\ldots,n}\subset\mathbb{C}, we want to build up a solution uu of the rrth MCH flow MCHr​(u)=0\mathrm{MCH}_{r}(u)=0 such that u⁡(t0,r)=u(0)u(t_{0,r})=u^{(0)} for some t0,r∈ℂ,r∈ℕ0t_{0,r}\in\mathbb{C},~r\in\mathbb{N}_{0}.

We employ the following notation V~r,\widetilde{V}_{r}, F~r,\widetilde{F}_{r}, G~r,\widetilde{G}_{r}, H~r,\widetilde{H}_{r}, f~2​s\tilde{f}_{2s}, g~2​s,\tilde{g}_{2s}, h~2​s\tilde{h}_{2s} to stand for the time-dependent quantities, which are obtained in Vn,V_{n}, Fn,F_{n}, Gn,G_{n}, Hn,H_{n}, f2​l,f_{2l}, g2​l,g_{2l}, h2​lh_{2l} by replacing {cl}l=1,…,n\{c_{l}\}_{l=1,\ldots,n} with {c~s}s=1,…,r\{\tilde{c}_{s}\}_{s=1,\ldots,r}, where the integration constants {cl}l=1,…,n⊂ℂ\{c_{l}\}_{l=1,\ldots,n}\subset\mathbb{C} in the stationary MCH hierarchy and {c~s}s=1,…,r⊂ℂ\{\tilde{c}_{s}\}_{s=1,\ldots,r}\subset\mathbb{C} in the time-dependent MCH hierarchy are independent of each other. In addition, we mark the individual rrth MCH flow by a separate time variable tr∈ℂt_{r}\in\mathbb{C}.

6 Time-dependent algebro-geometric solutions

In this final section, we extend the results in section 4 from the stationary MCH hierarchy to the time-dependent case. In particular, we obtain Riemann theta function representations for the Baker-Akhiezer function, the meromorphic function ϕ\phi, and the algebro-geometric solutions for the MCH hierarchy.

Let us first consider the asymptotic properties of ϕ\phi in the time-dependent case.

Lemma 6.1

Next, we study the properties of Abel map, which dose not linearize the divisor 𝒟μ¯^​(x,tr)\mathcal{D}_{\underline{\hat{\mu}}(x,t_{r})} and 𝒟ν¯^​(x,tr)\mathcal{D}_{\underline{\hat{\nu}}(x,t_{r})} in the time-dependent MCH hierarchy. This is the remarkable difference between the MCH hierarchy and other integrable systems such as KdV and AKNS hierarchies. For that purpose, we introduce some notations of symmetric functions.

𝒮k={l¯=(l1,…,ln)∈ℕk|l1<⋯<lk≤n},k=1,…,n,𝒯k(j)={l¯=(l1,…,ln)∈𝒮k|lm≠j},k=1,…,n−1,j=1,…,n.\begin{split}\mathcal{S}_{k}&=\{\underline{l}=(l_{1},\ldots,l_{n})\in\mathbb{N}^{k}|~l_{1}<\cdots<l_{k}\leq n\},\quad k=1,\ldots,n,\\ \mathcal{T}_{k}^{(j)}&=\{\underline{l}=(l_{1},\ldots,l_{n})\in\mathcal{S}_{k}|~l_{m}\neq j\},\quad k=1,\ldots,n-1,~j=1,\ldots,n.\end{split} (6.3)

Ψ0(μ¯)=1,Ψk(μ¯)=(−1)k∑l¯∈𝒮kμl1⋯μlk,k=1,…,n,\Psi_{0}(\underline{\mu})=1,\quad\Psi_{k}(\underline{\mu})=(-1)^{k}\sum_{\underline{l}\in\mathcal{S}_{k}}\mu_{l_{1}}\cdots\mu_{l_{k}},\quad k=1,\ldots,n, (6.4)

and

Theorem 6.4

Remark 4.84.8 is applicable to the present time-dependent context. Let us end this section by providing another principle result about algebro-geometric initial value problem of the MCH hierarchy. We will show that the solvability of the Dubrovin equations (5.60) and (5.61) on Ωμ⊆ℂ2\Omega_{\mu}\subseteq\mathbb{C}^{2} in fact implies (5.3) and (5.4) on Ωμ\Omega_{\mu}. As pointed out in Remark 4.13, this amounts to solving the time-dependent algebro-geometric initial value problem (5.1) and (5.2) on Ωμ\Omega_{\mu}. Recalling definition of F~r​(μj)\widetilde{F}_{r}(\mu_{j}) introduced in (6.6), then we may present the following result.

Assume that (2.2)(\ref{2.2}) holds and {μ^j}j=1,…,n\{\hat{\mu}_{j}\}_{j=1,\ldots,n} satisfies the Dubrovin equations (5.60)(\ref{5.60}) and (5.61)(\ref{5.61}) on Ωμ\Omega_{\mu} and remain distinct and nonzero for (x,tr)∈Ωμ(x,t_{r})\in\Omega_{\mu}, where Ωμ⊆ℂ2\Omega_{\mu}\subseteq\mathbb{C}^{2} is open and connected. If F~r​(μj)\widetilde{F}_{r}(\mu_{j}) in (5.61)(\ref{5.61}) are expressed in terms of μk\mu_{k}, k=1,…,nk=1,\ldots,n by (6.6)(\ref{6.6}), then u∈C∞​(Ωμ)u\in C^{\infty}(\Omega_{\mu}) satisfying

with initial values satisfying the nnth stationary MCH equation (5.2)(5.2).

Remark 6.10

The result in Theorem 6.96.9 is presented in terms of uu and {μj}j=1,⋯,n\{\mu_{j}\}_{j=1,\cdots,n}, but of course one can provide the analogous result in terms of uu and {νj}j=1,⋯,n\{\nu_{j}\}_{j=1,\cdots,n}.

The analog of Remark 4.13 directly extends to the current time-dependent MCH hierarchy.
